questions.stem: The Anti-Defection Law in India is contained in which Schedule of the Constitution?
questions.explanation: Anti-Defection Law is in the Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985. It prevents elected members from switching parties after winning elections.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Under the Tenth Schedule, a member of Parliament or State Legislature is disqualified if they:

options.option_text: Voluntarily give up membership of their political party
Vote against the government on a confidence motion

questions.explanation: Disqualification triggers: (1) voluntarily giving up party membership; (2) voting against the party's direction (whip) or abstaining without party permission. Mere criticism does not attract disqualification.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Who is the authority to decide disqualification questions under the Tenth Schedule?

options.option_text: The Speaker/Chairman of the respective House

questions.explanation: Under the Tenth Schedule, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha / Vidhan Sabha or Chairman of the Rajya Sabha / Vidhan Parishad is the deciding authority for disqualification petitions.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Tenth Schedule originally allowed a merger to be valid if — members of a legislative party joined another party.
questions.explanation: The original Tenth Schedule (1985) allowed defection by merger if at least 1/3 of the legislative party joined together. This 1/3 exception was deleted by the 91st Amendment (2003), raising the threshold to 2/3.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) changed the merger threshold under the Tenth Schedule to:
questions.explanation: The 91st Amendment (2003) amended the Tenth Schedule: now a valid merger requires at least two-thirds of the legislative party's members joining another party. The earlier one-third threshold was considered too easy to exploit.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Anti-Defection Law was enacted primarily to:

options.option_text: Increase political stability by preventing 'aaya ram gaya ram' culture of floor-crossing
Allow parties to dismiss disloyal ministers
Give the Speaker veto power over legislation

questions.explanation: The law was a response to rampant floor-crossing (termed 'aaya ram gaya ram' after Gaya Lal, a Haryana MLA who changed parties multiple times in one day in 1967), causing frequent government falls.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Speaker's decision on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule is subject to:

options.option_text: Judicial review by High Courts and Supreme Court

questions.explanation: In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court held that Speaker's decisions under the Tenth Schedule are JUDICIAL in nature and subject to judicial review, though courts will not interfere until the final order.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which category of persons is EXEMPT from disqualification under the Tenth Schedule?

options.option_text: Members elected on party ticket who later form a new party
Speaker/Chairman (elected by the House) who has resigned from their party

questions.explanation: Speakers/Chairmen who resign from their party upon assuming the constitutional office are exempt from disqualification — their office demands impartiality above party loyalty.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Tenth Schedule was added to the Constitution by which amendment?
questions.explanation: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 added the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) to the Constitution. It amended Articles 101, 102, 190, and 191 as well.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Under which circumstances does the Anti-Defection Law NOT apply to a member's vote?

options.option_text: When the member votes based on conscience
When the party's whip is not issued
When the House is in recess
When the member has been absent for 60 days

questions.explanation: If a party does not issue a whip (direction) on a particular vote, members are free to vote independently. Disqualification only applies when a member votes against or abstains contrary to a party whip.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The term 'voluntarily given up membership' under the Tenth Schedule has been interpreted to include:

options.option_text: Only formal written resignation from the party
Acting against the party (e.g., joining rival election campaigns) even without formal resignation

questions.explanation: Courts have held that 'voluntarily giving up membership' is wider than formal resignation. Supporting a rival candidate, attending hostile party functions, or publicly working against the party can also constitute this.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: If a member of the Rajya Sabha votes contrary to the party whip, the disqualification petition is decided by the:
questions.explanation: For Rajya Sabha members, the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is the deciding authority. For Lok Sabha, it is the Speaker. For State Assemblies, it is the Speaker; for State Councils, the Chairman.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: A nominated member of a House who is not a member of any political party may join a political party within how many days of taking the oath?
questions.explanation: Nominated members who are not affiliated to any party may join a party within 6 months of taking their seat without attracting disqualification. After 6 months, any party affiliation triggers potential disqualification rules.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Anti-Defection Law primarily curtails which feature of parliamentary democracy?

options.option_text: Parliamentary freedom to vote according to conscience (free vote)

questions.explanation: Critics argue the Anti-Defection Law undermines individual parliamentary freedom (free vote) by binding members to party whips on every issue. However, it promotes stability and prevents opportunistic switching.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct statement about the Anti-Defection Law?

options.option_text: It applies to all votes in Parliament
A Speaker can be disqualified for defection by another Speaker
The law prevents parties from expelling members
It was first enacted in 1975 during the Emergency

questions.explanation: If a Speaker themselves defects, the other House can pass a resolution under Article 94 (Lok Sabha) / 90 (RS) removing them. The Speaker cannot decide their own disqualification — a conflict of interest addressed in Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: What is 'merger' under the Tenth Schedule?

options.option_text: Two parties uniting at the national level
When at least 2/3 of a legislative party's members join another party or form a new party
When a party's symbol is changed
When an alliance is formed before elections

questions.explanation: Under the Tenth Schedule, 'merger' means at least 2/3 of the legislative party's strength merges with another party. This does not attract disqualification. Less than 2/3 is treated as defection.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Anti-Defection Law applies to:

options.option_text: Both Members of Parliament and Members of State Legislatures

questions.explanation: The Tenth Schedule applies to both Parliament (Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha) and all State Legislatures (Legislative Assemblies and Legislative Councils). The deciding authority is the presiding officer of each House.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which landmark case led to the Supreme Court calling for an independent tribunal instead of the Speaker deciding defection cases?
questions.explanation: In Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker of Arunachal Pradesh Assembly (2016), the Supreme Court highlighted the conflict of interest when the Speaker (who is a party member) decides cases against members of rival parties. The court suggested an independent tribunal.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: If a member is disqualified under the Tenth Schedule, they:

options.option_text: Cannot be minister in that House but can remain a member
Lose their seat and become ineligible to vote or contest for that term
Lose their seat in the House

questions.explanation: Disqualification under the Tenth Schedule means the member loses their seat (becomes disqualified to be a member of the House). However, they can contest elections to the same seat.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 'whip' in parliamentary terminology refers to:

options.option_text: A physical instrument used in Parliament
An official direction issued by a party to its members about how to vote
The presiding officer of the House

questions.explanation: A 'whip' is a written directive from a political party to its members in the legislature instructing them to be present and vote in a specific way. A three-line whip is the most binding; voting against it attracts disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
questions.subject: Polity
